metric.why: A facility can have enough total cooling and still starve individual racks; airflow and pressure sensors find recirculation, bypass, and leaks that temperature averages hide.
metric.definition: Cubic feet per minute delivered through the room or containment system, and the pressure differential that drives it through equipment rather than around it.

reading.body:
Airflow volume and static pressure reveal cooling failures that average temperatures cannot detect, because air can bypass equipment entirely rather than passing through it.

Data centers measure temperature across a room and assume uniform cooling. This misses the actual problem: air taking paths of least resistance, recirculating already-warm exhaust, or leaking around containment barriers. Static pressure, the force driving air through the equipment rather than around it, is the metric that catches these inefficiencies. A facility can have adequate total cooling capacity and still starve individual racks of the airflow they need.

For AI infrastructure, this matters because high-density compute racks demand precise airflow control. Recirculation or bypass reduces effective cooling capacity without adding infrastructure, which means some racks run hotter than their specifications allow. This forces either underutilization of expensive equipment or accelerated hardware degradation. The binding constraint becomes not total power delivered to the building, but power actually usable at the rack level.

The data does not specify which types of compute racks or cooling architectures are most vulnerable to airflow problems, nor does it quantify the efficiency losses that result from poor static pressure management.
